audits.mathematicalReason: External tangency makes the distance from the central center to each outer center R = r + 1, while adjacent outer centers are distance 2 apart. The closed ring therefore gives a regular dodecagon with central angle 30°. Bisecting one central triangle gives R sin(15°) = 1. The double-angle identity and positive square-root branch yield R = √6 + √2. Alternatively, projections at 30° and Pythagoras give 4 = R²[(1 − √3/2)² + (1/2)²] = R²(2 − √3), with the same positive value of R. Thus a = 6, b = 2, c = −1, and their sum is 7. Both candidate routes are valid alternatives.

routes.label: Arc subtraction and completing the square

audits.mathematicalReason: Let x = OA and let θ be the minor angle between the two rays, measured in radians. The outer radius is x + 2π. The two arc equations are (x + 2π)θ = 2π and x(2π − θ) = 2π, so 1/x + 1/(x + 2π) = 1. Consequently x² + (2π − 2)x − 2π = 0, or (x + π − 1)² = π² + 1. The negative root is inadmissible. The positive root lies between 1 and 2 and gives 0 < θ < π, consistent with the specified major and minor arcs. The arc equations can also be combined directly to obtain x + θ = 2 and then the same quadratic, supporting the subtraction/completing-square route without requiring the rational-equation route.

audits.mathematicalReason: For bottom entries a, b, c, the top entry is (a + b) + (b + c) = a + 2b + c. Because the digits are distinct and belong to 1 through 9, a + b + c ≥ 6 and b ≥ 1, giving a minimum of at least 7; bottom entries (2, 1, 3) attain it. Similarly, a + b + c ≤ 24 and b ≤ 9, giving a maximum of at most 33; bottom entries (7, 9, 8) attain it. The difference is 33 − 7 = 26. These are universal bounds with attaining constructions, matching the assessed extremal scope.

audits.mathematicalReason: Color the seven columns alternately. There are 12 cells of one color and 9 of the other. Every 2×2 tile and every horizontal 1×4 tile covers two cells of each color; a vertical 1×4 tile cannot fit. Thus unit tiles must account for imbalance 3, requiring at least three of them. Area also gives m ≡ 21 ≡ 1 (mod 4), so m ≥ 5. This is attainable: cover the first four columns with one horizontal 1×4 tile in each row, then place a 2×2 tile in the remaining 3×3 region and fill its five remaining cells with unit tiles. The packing route is independently valid: at most three 2×2 tiles fit because all meet the middle row, and at most one bar fits in each row. With two 2×2 tiles no middle-row bar fits; with three, pigeonhole forces two squares to meet one outer row, excluding a bar there as well as in the middle row. Hence at most four area-4 tiles fit, again requiring at least five unit tiles.

audits.mathematicalReason: Under the intended equal-width reading, let a square tile have side s. A 3s-by-3s repeating block contains four corner square tiles, so the pentagons occupy 9s² − 4s² = 5s². Their percentage is 100·5/9 ≈ 55.56%, closest to 56. The supplied scopes correctly describe this conditional calculation. However, the same incidence pattern can be formed with square side s and intervening strip width t: a repeating block then has side 2s + t, four corner squares, and four mutually congruent pentagons. Its pentagon fraction is 1 − 4s²/(2s + t)², which varies with t. For example, t = 0.9s gives about 52.44%. Thus the unmarked equality t = s is consequential rather than derivable merely from congruence.
